title: Book VII: Two Temptations — Chapter LXIV
paragraphs: 1_st Gent_. Where lies the power, there let the blame lie too.

2_d Gent_. Nay, power is relative; you cannot fright
The coming pest with border fortresses,
Or catch your carp with subtle argument.
All force is twain in one: cause is not cause
Unless effect be there; and action’s self
Must needs contain a passive. So command
Exists but with obedience.

Even if Lydgate had wanted to speak freely about his affairs, he knew Farebrother could scarcely have supplied the help he needed at once. The year's bills were arriving from tradesmen. Dover's claim on his furniture hung over him. His only dependable income was the slow trickle of payments from patients he must take care not to offend: the generous fees from Freshitt Hall and Lowick Manor had been swallowed up readily enough. Nothing short of a thousand pounds would clear his immediate difficulties and leave a little over to give him, in the hopeful phrase people favor in such situations, “time to look about him.”

Merry Christmas and the happy New Year naturally brought the moment when fellow citizens expected payment for the goods and services they had smilingly supplied. These sordid cares now pressed so tightly on Lydgate's mind that he could scarcely think continuously about anything else, however familiar or compelling. He was not bad-tempered by nature. His active intellect, warmhearted kindness, and strong constitution would ordinarily have kept him above the petty, uncontrolled sensitivities that produce bad temper. But he was suffering from the worst kind of irritation. Beneath each annoyance lay another awareness: that he was wasting his energy on a degrading preoccupation, the opposite of everything he had once intended. “_This_ is what occupies me, and _that_ is what might have occupied me,” ran the bitter, unceasing murmur within. Every difficulty therefore pricked his impatience twice.

Some gentlemen have achieved remarkable literary reputations by expressing general dissatisfaction with a universe they consider a trap of dullness into which their great souls fell by mistake. But the sense of an enormous self in an insignificant world may offer consolations. Lydgate's dissatisfaction was harder to bear. He felt that a grand life of thought and useful action lay all around him, while his own life shrank into the miserable solitude of selfish fears and commonplace anxieties about events that might relieve them. His troubles may seem pitifully sordid, beneath the notice of elevated people who understand debt only on a magnificent scale. Sordid they certainly were. For the majority, who are not elevated, the only escape from such sordidness is freedom from craving money, with all its low hopes and temptations: waiting for someone to die, hinting at requests, wanting like a horse dealer to pass off bad work as good, seeking a post that ought to belong to someone else, and often being driven to long for a stroke of Luck in the shape of a widespread disaster.

Lydgate's horror at putting his neck under this degrading yoke had plunged him into the bitter mood that kept widening the distance between him and Rosamond. Since first telling her about the bill of sale, he had repeatedly tried to win her sympathy for ways of reducing their expenses. As Christmas approached threateningly, his suggestions became more definite. “The two of us can manage with one servant and live on very little,” he said. “And I can do with one horse.” As we have seen, he was beginning to think more clearly about living costs. Whatever pride he took in such outward appearances was slight compared with the pride that recoiled from being exposed as a debtor or asking other men for money.

“Of course you can dismiss the other two servants if you wish,” Rosamond said. “But I should have thought living poorly would damage your standing considerably. You must expect your practice to suffer.”

“My dear Rosamond, we don't have a choice. We started too expensively. Peacock lived in a much smaller house, you know. It's my fault. I should have known better. I deserve a beating, if anyone had the right to give me one, for forcing you to live with less than you're used to. But I suppose we married because we loved each other. That may help us get through until things improve. Come, darling, put your work down and come here.”

At that moment his feelings about her were cold and gloomy. Yet he dreaded a future without affection and was determined to resist the growing separation between them. Rosamond did as he asked, and he drew her onto his knee, though inwardly she remained utterly distant. The poor woman saw only that the world had not arranged itself to please her, and Lydgate was part of that world. He held her waist with one hand and gently laid the other over both of hers. This rather abrupt man could be very tender toward women, as though always conscious of their fragile bodies and the delicate balance of their physical and mental health. He began again, trying to persuade her.

“Now that I'm looking into things, Rosy, I'm astonished how much money disappears into the housekeeping. I suppose the servants are careless, and we've entertained a great many people. But plenty of people in our position must manage on much less. I suppose they use simpler things and keep an eye on leftovers. Money doesn't seem to go far in these matters. Wrench keeps everything as plain as possible, and he has an enormous practice.”
“If you're thinking of living like the Wrenches!” Rosamond said, turning her neck slightly. “I've heard you say how much you dislike their way of life.”
“Yes, their taste is dreadful in everything. They make saving money look ugly. We don't have to do that. I only meant that they avoid expense despite his excellent practice.”

“Why shouldn't your practice be good, Tertius? Mr. Peacock's was. You ought to take more care not to offend people and supply medicines as the others do. You certainly started well and secured several good households. Being eccentric can't pay. You should consider what people generally like.” Rosamond spoke with a small, definite note of correction.

Lydgate felt his anger rise. He was willing to indulge feminine weakness, but not feminine authority. A water sprite's shallow soul may seem charming until she starts giving lessons. He controlled himself, however, and said only, with a touch of commanding firmness—

“How I conduct my practice is for me to decide, Rosy. That isn't what we're discussing. You need only understand that our income will probably be very small for a long time—barely four hundred pounds, perhaps less. We must try to arrange our lives accordingly.”
Rosamond looked straight ahead in silence for a moment, then said, “My uncle Bulstrode ought to pay you a salary for the time you spend at the Hospital. It isn't right for you to work for nothing.”

“Everyone understood from the start that I would work without payment. That needn't come into this discussion either. I've told you the only likely prospect,” Lydgate said impatiently. Then he checked himself and continued more quietly—

“I think there's one way of freeing ourselves from a good part of the immediate difficulty. I hear young Ned Plymdale is marrying Sophy Toller. They're wealthy, and good houses don't often become available in Middlemarch. I'm sure they'd be glad to take this one with most of our furniture, and pay a handsome sum for the lease. I could ask Trumbull to approach Plymdale.”

Rosamond got off his knee and walked slowly to the far end of the room. When she turned back toward him, he could see tears in her eyes. She bit her lower lip and clasped her hands to stop herself from crying. Lydgate felt miserable, shaken by anger but certain it would be unmanly to let it out just then.
“I'm so sorry, Rosamond. I know how painful this is.”
“I thought that after I'd endured sending the silver back and having that man make a list of the furniture—surely _that_ should have been enough.”

“I explained then, darling. That was only security. Behind the security is a debt, and we have to pay it within the next few months or the furniture will be sold. If young Plymdale takes the house and most of the furniture, we can pay that debt and some others, and escape a place we can't afford. We could rent a smaller house. Trumbull has a perfectly decent one for thirty pounds a year, I know, while this costs ninety.” Lydgate delivered this in the short, hammering manner people use to pin a vague mind to unavoidable facts. Tears silently ran down Rosamond's cheeks. She merely pressed her handkerchief against them and stood staring at the large vase on the mantel. She had never felt such intense bitterness. At last she said slowly, emphasizing each word with care—
“I could never have believed you'd want to behave like this.”

“Want to?” Lydgate burst out. He rose, thrust his hands into his pockets, and strode away from the hearth. “It isn't about what I want. Of course I don't want it. It's the only thing I can do.” He wheeled around to face her.
“I should have thought there were plenty of other ways,” Rosamond replied. “Let's sell everything and leave Middlemarch altogether.”
“And do what? What good would it do to leave my work here for somewhere I have none? We'd be just as penniless anywhere else,” Lydgate said, angrier still.

“If that's the position we're to be in, Tertius, it will be entirely your own fault,” Rosamond said, turning to him with complete conviction. “You refuse to treat your family as you should. You offended Captain Lydgate. Sir Godwin was very kind to me at Quallingham. I'm sure that if you showed him proper respect and explained your situation, he'd do anything for you. But you prefer handing our house and furniture over to Mr. Ned Plymdale.”

Something fierce entered Lydgate's eyes. He answered with renewed violence, “Very well, if you insist, I do prefer it. I admit I'd rather do that than make a fool of myself begging where it will do no good. Understand, then: it is what I _want to do_.”

His tone in that last sentence was like the grip of his strong hand on Rosamond's delicate arm. Yet his will was no stronger than hers. She immediately left the room without speaking, intensely determined to prevent him from doing what he wanted.

He went out of the house. As his blood cooled, he realized that the conversation had chiefly left him dreading future discussions with his wife that might drive him into angry speech again. A crack seemed to have opened in delicate crystal, and he feared any movement that might break it beyond repair. Unless they could continue loving each other, his marriage would become a bitter joke. He had long ago accepted what he saw as her passive failings: her lack of sensitivity, shown in her disregard for both his particular wishes and his larger purposes. He had endured the first great disappointment. He must give up the tender devotion and obedient adoration of an ideal wife and resume life with lower expectations, like a man who has lost a limb. But his real wife still had both a claim upon him and a hold on his heart, and he desperately wanted that hold to remain strong. In marriage, the certainty “She will never love me much” is easier to bear than the fear “I shall stop loving her.” After his outburst, therefore, all his inward effort went into excusing her and blaming the hard circumstances for which he was partly responsible. That evening he tried through affection to heal the morning's wound. Rosamond was not naturally sulky or repellent. Indeed, she welcomed signs that her husband loved her and could be controlled. But this was quite different from loving _him_. Lydgate would have preferred not to return soon to the plan of giving up the house. He meant to carry it out with as little further discussion as possible. Yet Rosamond herself raised it over breakfast, asking gently—
“Have you spoken to Trumbull?”

“Not yet,” Lydgate said, “but I'll stop in as I pass this morning. We mustn't waste time.” He took the question as a sign that her inward resistance had ended, and kissed her head tenderly as he rose to leave.

As soon as visiting hours allowed, Rosamond went to Mrs. Plymdale, Ned's mother, and introduced the coming wedding with graceful congratulations. From a mother's perspective, Mrs. Plymdale thought Rosamond might now be seeing glimpses of her past foolishness. Since every advantage presently lay with her son, she was too kind a woman not to behave graciously.

“Yes, I must say Ned is wonderfully happy. And Sophy Toller is everything I could wish for in a daughter-in-law. Naturally her father can provide handsomely for her. With a brewery like his, that's only to be expected. The family connection is all we could desire too. But that's not what matters to me. She's such a nice girl, without airs or pretensions, though she's equal to the finest. I don't mean the titled aristocracy. I see little good in people reaching outside their own sphere. Sophy is as good as anyone in town, and she's content with that.”
“I've always found her very pleasant,” Rosamond said.

“I consider it a reward for Ned, who has never held his head too high, that he's made the very best connection,” Mrs. Plymdale continued. The warmth of her conviction that this was the correct view softened her natural sharpness. “The Tollers are so particular, they might have objected to our having friends they don't share. Everyone knows your aunt Bulstrode and I have been close since we were girls, and Mr. Plymdale has always supported Mr. Bulstrode. I prefer serious religious opinions myself. But the Tollers have welcomed Ned regardless.”
“I'm sure he's a very deserving young man with excellent principles,” Rosamond replied, neatly returning a little condescension for Mrs. Plymdale's wholesome corrections.

“Oh, he hasn't an army captain's style, or that way of carrying himself as though everyone else were beneath him, or those showy gifts for conversation, singing, and intellectual display. I'm thankful he hasn't. Such things prepare a man poorly for both this life and the next.”
“Oh, certainly. Appearances have very little to do with happiness,” said Rosamond. “I think they have every prospect of being happy together. What house will they have?”

“Well, they'll have to take what they can find. They've looked at the house in St. Peter's Place next door to Mr. Hackbutt. It belongs to him, and he's having it put in good repair. I doubt they'll hear of anything better. In fact, I think Ned will settle it today.”
“It must be a nice house. I like St. Peter's Place.”

“It's close to the church, and a respectable address. But the windows are narrow and the whole place is full of stairs and changes of level. You don't happen to know of another house becoming available?” Mrs. Plymdale fixed her round black eyes on Rosamond, animated by the sudden thought.
“Oh, no. I hear so little about such things.”

When Rosamond set out, she had not anticipated this question or her answer. She had only meant to gather information that would help her avoid losing her own house under circumstances she thoroughly disliked. She reflected no more on the lie she had just told than on the untruth of saying appearances had little to do with happiness. Her purpose, she was certain, was wholly justified. Lydgate's intention was the inexcusable one. She had a plan which, once completed, would prove how mistaken he would have been to lower himself from his present position.

On her way home she passed Borthrop Trumbull's office, intending to call. For the first time in her life, she was contemplating something in the nature of business, but she felt equal to it. The prospect of being forced to do something she intensely disliked turned her quiet persistence into active ingenuity. Here, mere disobedience and serene obstinacy would not suffice. She must act on her judgment, and she assured herself that her judgment was correct: “Indeed, if it weren't, I wouldn't want to act on it.”

Trumbull was in his back office and received her with his finest manners. Her charms appealed strongly to him, but kindness also stirred him. He knew Lydgate was in difficulties, and this exceptionally pretty woman, this young lady of the greatest personal attractions, would probably feel the pinch of trouble and find herself caught in circumstances beyond her control. He begged her to honor him by sitting down. Standing before her, he adjusted himself and his clothes with eager concern that was chiefly benevolent. Rosamond first asked whether her husband had called that morning about disposing of their house.

“Yes, ma'am, yes, he has. Indeed he has,” the kindly auctioneer said, trying to make the repetition soothing. “I intended to carry out his instructions this afternoon, if possible. He asked me not to delay.”
“I've come to ask you to take no further steps, Mr. Trumbull. And please don't mention anything that's been said about it. Will you do that for me?”

“Certainly, Mrs. Lydgate, certainly. I regard a confidence as sacred, whether in business or anything else. Then I should consider my instructions withdrawn?” He straightened the long ends of his blue cravat with both hands and looked at her respectfully.

“Yes, please. I've learned that Mr. Ned Plymdale has taken the house in St. Peter's Place next to Mr. Hackbutt. Mr. Lydgate would be annoyed to have his instructions carried out to no purpose. Besides, other circumstances have made the proposal unnecessary.”

“Very good, Mrs. Lydgate, very good. Whenever you need my services, I'm at your disposal,” Trumbull said, pleased to imagine that new resources had become available. “Please rely on me. The matter will go no further.”

That evening Lydgate found some comfort in Rosamond's being livelier than she had recently been. She even seemed interested in pleasing him without being asked. “If she's happy and I can struggle through, what does any of it matter?” he thought. “It's only a narrow swamp on a long journey. If I can clear my mind again, I'll manage.”

His improved spirits led him to search for an account of experiments he had long meant to consult. He had neglected it through the creeping loss of faith in himself that follows petty anxieties. Some of his old pleasure in absorption returned as he pursued a question with broad implications. Rosamond played quiet music, as helpful to his thinking as an oar's splash on an evening lake. It had grown late. He pushed the books aside and sat looking at the fire, hands clasped behind his head, forgetting everything except how to devise a new experiment to test his ideas. Rosamond had left the piano and was watching him from her chair when she said—
“Mr. Ned Plymdale has already taken a house.”
Startled and jarred, Lydgate looked up and was silent for a moment, like someone woken abruptly from sleep. Then, flushing as the unwelcome situation came back to him, he asked—
“How did you hear that?”
“I visited Mrs. Plymdale this morning. She told me he'd taken the house in St. Peter's Place beside Mr. Hackbutt's.”

Lydgate said nothing. He brought his hands from behind his head and pressed them against the thick hair that, as usual, hung over his forehead, resting his elbows on his knees. Bitter disappointment seized him, as though he had opened a door out of a suffocating room only to find it bricked up. He was also certain that Rosamond welcomed the cause of his distress. He preferred neither to look at her nor to speak until the first spasm of frustration had passed. After all, he thought bitterly, what could a woman care for as much as a house and furniture? A husband without them was ridiculous. When he finally looked up and pushed back his hair, his dark eyes held a miserable emptiness that expected no sympathy. He only said coolly—
“Someone else may come along. I asked Trumbull to keep looking if Plymdale wouldn't take it.”

Rosamond said nothing. She trusted to the chance that her husband and the auctioneer would not speak again until events had justified her interference. In any case, she had prevented the thing she immediately feared. After a pause she asked—
“How much money do those disagreeable people want?”
“Which disagreeable people?”
“The ones who made the list, and the others. How much would satisfy them so they wouldn't trouble you anymore?”

Lydgate studied her a moment as if checking for symptoms. “Well, if Plymdale had paid six hundred for the furniture and the lease, I might have managed. I could have cleared Dover's bill and paid enough toward the others to make them patient, provided we reduced our expenses.”
“But how much would you need if we stayed here?”

“More than I'm likely to get anywhere,” Lydgate replied with a grating edge of sarcasm. It angered him that her mind wandered among impossible wishes instead of facing efforts they could actually make.
“Why can't you tell me the amount?” Rosamond asked, mildly signaling her disapproval of his manners.
“Well,” he said, estimating, “at least a thousand would be needed to put me at ease. But,” he added sharply, “I have to think about managing without it, not with it.”
Rosamond let the matter drop.

The next day, however, she carried out her plan to write to Sir Godwin Lydgate. Since the Captain's visit, he had written to her, and so had his married sister, Mrs. Mengan. Both had expressed sympathy for the loss of her baby and a vague hope of seeing her at Quallingham again. Lydgate had told her these courtesies meant nothing. Secretly she remained convinced that any lack of warmth from his family was caused by his own coldness and contempt. She had answered the letters as charmingly as possible, fairly confident that a definite invitation would follow. Instead, there had been complete silence. The Captain was evidently no great letter writer, and perhaps the sisters had been abroad. Now, however, the season had arrived for thinking of friends at home. In any case Sir Godwin would surely be moved by her appeal. He had chucked her under the chin and compared her to the celebrated beauty Mrs. Croly, who had captivated him in 1790. For her sake he would find pleasure in behaving toward his nephew as he ought. Rosamond was innocently certain of an old gentleman's duty to save her from unpleasantness. She wrote what she considered an exceptionally sensible letter, one that would convince Sir Godwin of her excellent judgment. She explained how desirable it was for Tertius to leave a place like Middlemarch for somewhere better suited to his gifts, how the disagreeable inhabitants had obstructed his professional success, and how he had consequently fallen into financial difficulties from which a thousand pounds would completely free him. She did not mention that Tertius knew nothing of her intention to write. She thought his presumed approval would fit with her account of his great affection for Uncle Godwin as the relative who had always been his best friend. Such was poor Rosamond's skill at strategy now that she applied it to practical affairs.

All this preceded the New Year's Day party. No answer had yet arrived from Sir Godwin. But that morning Lydgate was to discover that Rosamond had canceled his instructions to Borthrop Trumbull. Believing she must gradually get used to the prospect of leaving their house in Lowick Gate, he overcame his reluctance to discuss it again. Over breakfast he said—

“I'll try to see Trumbull this morning and ask him to advertise the house in the ‘Pioneer’ and the ‘Trumpet.’ An advertisement might interest someone who hadn't considered moving. In country towns, people often stay in houses their families have outgrown simply because they don't know where to find another. Trumbull doesn't seem to have had a single inquiry.”
Rosamond knew the unavoidable moment had arrived. “I told Trumbull not to pursue it,” she said with a carefully controlled calm that was plainly defensive.

Lydgate stared, speechless with astonishment. Only half an hour earlier he had been fastening her braids and speaking the affectionate “little language” that Rosamond accepted without returning. She had been like a serene, lovely statue, occasionally rewarding its worshipper with a miraculous dimple. Those feelings still stirred in him, so the shock could not immediately become clear anger; it was a confused pain. He put down the carving knife and fork and leaned back in his chair. At last he said with cool irony—
“May I ask when you did this, and why?”

“When I heard the Plymdales had taken a house, I called to tell him not to offer ours. At the same time I told him to go no further. I knew it would harm you badly if people learned you wanted to give up your house and furniture, and I objected very strongly. I think that was reason enough.”

“So it didn't matter that I'd explained compelling reasons on the other side? It didn't matter that I'd reached a different decision and given instructions to match?” Lydgate spoke bitterly, his brow and eyes gathering thunder and lightning.
Other people's anger had always made Rosamond retreat into cold dislike and become still more calmly correct. Whatever anyone else might do, she was certain she would not misbehave. She answered—
“I think I had every right to speak about something that concerns me at least as much as it concerns you.”

“Certainly you had a right to speak—to me. You had no right to cancel my instructions behind my back and treat me like a fool,” Lydgate replied in the same tone. Then he added with greater scorn, “Can I possibly make you understand the consequences? Is there any point explaining again why we must try to give up the house?”

“You needn't tell me again,” Rosamond said, her voice falling like drops of cold water. “I remember what you said. You spoke just as violently then. But I still think you should try every other means before doing something so painful to me. And advertising the house would, I think, be completely degrading for you.”
“What if I ignore your opinion as you've ignored mine?”
“Of course you can. But before we married, you ought to have told me you'd put me in the worst possible position rather than give up your own way.”

Lydgate said nothing. He tossed his head sideways and the corners of his mouth twitched with despair. Seeing he was not looking at her, Rosamond rose and set his coffee in front of him. He ignored it, continuing an inward drama and argument. Now and then he shifted in his chair, rested an arm on the table, or rubbed his hair. Conflicting thoughts and feelings prevented him either from fully surrendering to anger or from simply holding firm to his resolve. Rosamond used his silence.

“When we married, everyone thought you had such a good position. I could never have imagined you'd want to sell our furniture and move to Bride Street, where the rooms are like cages. If we have to live that way, at least let's leave Middlemarch.”

“Those would be very powerful arguments,” Lydgate said with partial irony. His lips looked pale and shriveled as he stared at the coffee without drinking. “Very powerful, if I didn't happen to be in debt.”

“Plenty of people must have been in debt like this. If they're respectable, people trust them. I'm sure Papa said the Torbits were in debt, and they carried on perfectly well. Acting rashly can't be wise,” Rosamond said with serene authority.

Opposing impulses held Lydgate motionless. Since no argument seemed likely to win her agreement, he wanted to smash and grind some object on which he could at least make an impression, or brutally declare that he was the master and she must obey. Yet he feared more than the effect of such extremes on their life together. He was increasingly afraid of her quiet, slippery obstinacy, which would never let any assertion of power be final. She had also struck one of his most sensitive feelings by suggesting that marriage to him had cheated her with a false promise of happiness. As for declaring himself master, he was not. The resolution he had built through reasoning and honorable pride was already slackening under her numbing touch. He swallowed half his coffee and rose to leave.

“At least I can ask you not to go to Trumbull yet—not until we're certain there's no other way,” Rosamond said. Although she was not easily frightened, she thought it safer to conceal her letter to Sir Godwin. “Promise you won't see him for a few weeks, or without telling me.”
Lydgate gave a short laugh. “I think I'm the one who should demand a promise that you won't do anything without telling me.” He looked sharply at her, then moved toward the door.

“You remember we're dining at Papa's?” Rosamond said, hoping he would turn and give her a fuller concession. Instead he said impatiently, “Oh, yes,” and left. She thought it hateful of him to add an unpleasant temper to the painful proposals he had already made. When she asked so reasonably that he postpone another visit to Trumbull, it was cruel not to reassure her about his intentions. She was certain she had acted for the best in every respect. Each harsh or angry remark from him merely added another offense to her mental record. For months now, poor Rosamond had been associating her husband with disappointment. Marriage, that terribly inflexible relationship, had lost its charm as a source of delightful dreams. It had released her from the disagreeable features of her father's household but had not supplied everything she wished and hoped for. The Lydgate she loved had been, to her, a collection of airy circumstances. Most had vanished, replaced by daily details that had to be lived through slowly, hour by hour. She could no longer float through them by quickly selecting only their pleasing aspects. The demands of his profession, his absorption at home in scientific subjects—which seemed to her almost like a vampire's morbid appetite—and his peculiar opinions on matters never discussed during courtship all steadily estranged her. Even without his placing himself at a disadvantage in the town, even without the first shock of learning about Dover's debt, these influences would have made his company dull. From the early days of her marriage until four months ago, another person's presence had provided pleasant excitement, but that was gone. She would not admit how much the resulting emptiness contributed to her utter boredom. She thought, perhaps correctly, that an invitation to Quallingham and a chance for Lydgate to settle somewhere else—London, or any place likely to offer freedom from unpleasantness—would satisfy her entirely. Then she would not care about Will Ladislaw's absence. She felt some resentment toward him for making so much of Mrs. Casaubon.

This was how things stood between Lydgate and Rosamond when they dined at her father's on New Year's Day. Remembering his temper at breakfast, she appeared mildly indifferent to him. He bore much deeper effects from the inner struggle in which that morning's scene was only one episode among many. His flushed effort in talking to Farebrother, his attempt at the cynical claim that all ways of acquiring money were essentially alike and chance ruled so completely that choice was a fool's illusion, revealed a weakening resolution and a numbed response to his old enthusiasms.

What could he do? He saw even more clearly than Rosamond how dreary it would be to take her to the little Bride Street house, with scant furniture around her and resentment inside her. Ever since poverty had become a threat, life with Rosamond and life with deprivation had seemed increasingly impossible to combine. Even if determination forced those two pictures together, the practical steps needed for the hard change were nowhere in sight. Though he had not given his wife the promise she requested, he did not return to Trumbull. He even began considering a quick trip north to see Sir Godwin. Once he had thought nothing could make him ask his uncle for money, but he had not then experienced the full pressure of still worse alternatives. A letter's effect would be uncertain. Only a meeting, however unpleasant, would let him explain fully and test what family feeling might accomplish. Yet no sooner did he begin to picture this as the easiest course than anger flared again. He had long ago resolved to keep clear of such humiliating calculations, such self-interested worry about the inclinations and pockets of men whose purposes he had proudly refused to share. Now he had fallen not merely to their level but to the level of begging from them.
